direct_claims: This scatter plot, produced by Our World in Data using data from the UN World Population Prospects (2024), compares the sex ratio at birth against the sex ratio at five years old for various countries in the year 2023.
The data is categorized by continent, including North America, South America, Africa, Europe, Asia, and Oceania.
The y-axis measures the sex ratio at birth (males per 100 females), while the x-axis measures the sex ratio at age five (males per 100 females).
A grey diagonal line represents the point of equal ratio; countries lying above this line experienced a decrease in the male-to-female ratio between birth and age five.
derived_claims: The chart aims to illustrate how the proportion of males to females changes during the first five years of life across different global regions.
Most countries in the chart cluster around this biological norm, with birth ratios between 104 and 107 and age-five ratios between 103 and 106.
Countries like China, Azerbaijan, and Vietnam maintain exceptionally high sex ratios at both birth and age five (above 110 males per 100 females).
The visualization highlights regional patterns, showing that many African nations cluster at slightly lower sex ratios at birth (around 101 to 103) compared to the global average.
speculative_claims: Biologically, the natural human sex ratio at birth is slightly biased toward males, typically around 105 males per 100 females.
Under normal conditions, higher natural mortality rates among male infants and young children gradually reduce this ratio, bringing it closer to parity (100) by age five.
In demography, these highly skewed ratios are widely understood to reflect cultural preferences for sons combined with sex-selective practices and unequal healthcare access.

If these highly skewed male-biased trends continue, these societies face severe long-term consequences, such as a 'marriage squeeze' (a shortage of potential female partners) and potential social instability.

Extreme outliers in very small populations, such as Liechtenstein (with a birth ratio near 116) or Montserrat (with an age-five ratio near 73), are likely the result of statistical noise and annual fluctuations in small sample sizes rather than systemic demographic shifts.
